indian-coffee-house.blurb: The College Street Coffee House: a vast, high-ceilinged hall that has hosted Kolkata's students, poets and arguers for generations.

tips.expect: A noisy, nostalgic hall of tables where people argue over cheap coffee. Reported hours are 9 am to 9 pm, and it costs around ₹200 for two.
tips.good: The cutlet is a legend, and the coffee is old-fashioned and cheap. The history is the real draw.
tips.watch: Cash only. It's popular with students, so tables fill up in the late afternoon.
tips.tip: Combine it with College Square and the College Street book lanes. Go before 6 pm and get a table with a view of the hall.

flurys.blurb: The Park Street tearoom founded in 1927 by the Swiss couple Joseph and Frieda Flury, which taught Calcutta European cafe culture.

tips.expect: A bright old tearoom at 18 Park Street with a famous breakfast and a counter of cakes and pastries.
tips.good: Breakfast, and carrying home the rum balls and pastries.
tips.watch: Weekend mornings and Puja afternoons can mean a queue for a table.
tips.tip: Trincas, which was started by Flury's former partner, is diagonally opposite at 17 Park Street.

peter-cat.blurb: A Park Street restaurant open since 1975, with red sofas, red pendant lamps and waiters in Rajasthani dress.
dishes: Chelo kebab with buttered rice and a fried egg

tips.expect: A classic, slightly theatrical Park Street dinner. It is under the same management as Mocambo across the road.
tips.good: Chelo kebab, an Irani dish that Peter Cat introduced to Calcuttans, and the sizzlers.
tips.watch: There is a small Continental menu but it is better known for tandoori. Waits are long on Saturday nights.
tips.tip: Reserve on Puja weekends, or go for an early dinner before the crowd.

nizam-s.blurb: The restaurant in New Market (then Sir Stuart Hogg Market) where the kathi roll was invented, around 1932.

tips.expect: A busy old kebab house. The first roll was a kebab wrapped in paratha for a sahib who didn't want to eat with his hands.
tips.good: The original: skewered kebab, egg-layered paratha and chutney.
tips.watch: Rolls here are meaty and filling, so one is enough. It gets crowded around New Market shopping hours.
tips.tip: Other famous roll places for comparison: Kusum Rolls, Campari, Zeesha and Chacha Jaan.

aminia.blurb: A Mughlai and Awadhi institution that began on Zakaria Street in 1929. The New Market branch at 6A SN Banerjee Road has served biryani since 1947.
dishes: Kolkata-style biryani with potato and egg

tips.expect: A family restaurant with generations of regulars. Kolkata biryani comes with a soft potato and often a boiled egg.
tips.good: The biryani, and the mix of Mughlai and Awadhi dishes.
tips.watch: Peak lunch and dinner hours are busy, and Puja evenings more so.
tips.tip: Close to New Market and Esplanade, so it fits easily into the Central pandal plan.

royal-indian-hotel.blurb: An old Chitpur Mughlai restaurant that started in 1905 with mutton chaanp. It also has a Park Street branch.

tips.expect: A no-frills heritage eatery with big flavours.
tips.good: The chaanp, biryani and the sweet shahi tukda to finish.
tips.watch: The Chitpur original is in a crowded market area, so allow time to reach it.
tips.tip: The Park Street branch is easier if you are on that side of town.

arsalan.blurb: A Park Circus landmark, always busy, famous for its Kolkata chicken biryani with a saffron-hued potato.

tips.good: The chicken biryani with its soft potato.
tips.watch: Expect a wait at dinner, especially during Puja.
tips.tip: Go for an early or late dinner to avoid the queue.

k-c-das.blurb: The sweet shop founded in 1930 by Krishna Chandra Das, son of Nobin Chandra Das, the man credited with inventing the rosogolla in 1868.

tips.expect: A classic Kolkata sweet shop. The Esplanade East outlet was the first with uniformed staff and Western-style service.
tips.good: The rosogolla and the rasmalai, which K.C. Das is credited with creating.
tips.watch: Sweets sell out in the late evening.
tips.tip: Esplanade is the outlet to visit. Pick up a box on the way to the metro.

6-ballygunge-place.blurb: A Bengali restaurant opened in 2003 in a restored colonial bungalow, with a menu researched from food served in the Tagore household.

tips.expect: Sit-down Bengali dining in an old house, a cut above a Puja-night snack.
tips.good: The daab chingri and the kasha mangsho.
tips.tip: A good celebratory meal after the Ballygunge pandals.

kewpie-s-kitchen.blurb: A family-run Bengali restaurant on Elgin Road, in a small lane near Netaji's house, with the feel of a traditional Bengali home.

tips.expect: Home-cooked Bengali food led by chef Rakhi Purnima Dasgupta, served as thalis.
tips.good: The small terracotta dishes and the home-style cooking.
tips.watch: It is tucked in a lane, so look for it carefully. Reservations are a good idea.
tips.tip: Close to the Mallick Bari and Netaji Bhavan.

vivekananda-park-phuchka-stalls.blurb: The cluster of phuchka sellers around Vivekananda Park, Bhowanipore, often called the birthplace of Kolkata's phuchka culture.

tips.expect: Evening crowds around the stalls, with several well-known sellers such as Dilip Da's Puchka Centre and Maharaja Chat Centre.
tips.good: The variety: dahi phuchka, dum aloo phuchka and papri chaat in one place.
tips.watch: Street food hygiene varies. Go for stalls with a steady crowd and fresh water.
tips.tip: Best in the early evening, before the dinner rush.

adi-haridas-modak.blurb: A sweet shop at 220 Acharya Prafulla Chandra Road, Shyambazar, said to be about 250 years old and run today by the sixth generation of the Modak family.

tips.expect: A traditional Bengali breakfast spot and sweet shop at the Shyambazar five-point crossing.
tips.good: Hot kochuri and light potato curry for breakfast.
tips.watch: It is a breakfast and morning place, and much of the best is gone by midday.
tips.tip: Go early on Shashthi or Saptami before the day's pandal-hopping.

nobin-chandra-das.blurb: The Sovabazar sweet shop of the family of Nobin Chandra Das, who invented the rosogolla in 1868.

tips.expect: A heritage sweet shop with roots in Kolkata's food history.
tips.good: The sandesh and the rosogolla, and being at the source of the legend.
tips.watch: Closing times vary, so go before the evening rush.
tips.tip: It is two minutes from the Shobhabazar Rajbari. Buy a box before you start the bari walk.

golbari.blurb: A Shyambazar eatery of nearly a century, started as the New Punjabi Restaurant and named Golbari for its semicircular facade. It is known for kosha mangsho.

tips.expect: A busy old-Kolkata eatery at the five-point crossing.
tips.good: The kosha mangsho, a slow-cooked, dry mutton curry.
tips.watch: It is crowded at lunch and dinner.
tips.tip: Combine with Adi Haridas Modak in a Shyambazar food stop.
